Spatial and Range Feasibility Pre-Filter.definition: Precompute binary feasibility indicators for each site or origin-facility pair. Incorporate them by either restricting the candidate set or adding constraints y_j ≤ feasible_j and x_{ij} ≤ allowed_{ij}⋅M. This eliminates infeasible options and avoids embedding complex spatial or nonlinear distance checks directly in the MIP.
Spatial and Range Feasibility Pre-Filter.condition: When candidate facility sites or arcs are subject to multiple geometric or distance-based feasibility constraints (obstacles, setbacks, geofences, roof area, maximum range) that can be evaluated offline before optimization.

Multimodal Linkage Constraints.definition: Pre-filter assignment variables by ground travel time ≤ T_max. For remote sites, incorporate a binary opening variable with cost and time penalty; incorporate penalty in assignment time bound using big-M. Objective includes fixed transit extension cost.
Multimodal Linkage Constraints.condition: When facilities serve as intermodal transfer points with ground connectivity, and some candidate sites are remote, requiring a transit extension that adds a fixed cost and a travel time penalty.

Remote Site Transit Extension Cost and T.definition: Pre-filter assignment variables by ground travel time ≤ T_max. For remote sites, incorporate a binary opening variable with cost and time penalty; incorporate penalty in assignment time bound using big-M. Objective includes fixed transit extension cost.
Remote Site Transit Extension Cost and T.condition: When facilities serve as intermodal transfer points with ground connectivity, and some candidate sites are remote, requiring a transit extension that adds a fixed cost and a travel time penalty.

Logit Choice with Perceptible Benefit Th.definition: Activate the logit share only if the time saving exceeds the threshold. Use a binary indicator z_i = 1 if time_saving_i ≥ threshold, enforced by logical constraints. Allocate demand proportional to z_i⋅exp(V_i)/Σ_j z_j⋅exp(V_j). Replace the logit exponential with piecewise-linear segments to maintain MILP tractability.
Logit Choice with Perceptible Benefit Th.condition: When demand follows a logit choice model and users exhibit a minimum perceptible benefit threshold (e.g., 25% time saving) before switching, causing nonlinearity when utility depends on decision variables.

Capacity and Footprint from Design Decis.definition: Model throughput as a linear function of design variables: throughput ≤ Σ (per‑unit capacity)·design_var. Derive achievable throughput from a queuing model (e.g., M/D/n) as a concave function g(pad_count) and embed via piecewise-linear segments: total arrivals ≤ g(pad_count). Enforce footprint: total area ≥ base + β·throughput; sum functional areas ≤ total area, with lower bounds from throughput. Use big-M to coup...
Capacity and Footprint from Design Decis.condition: When facility throughput capacity, physical footprint, and functional area allocations depend on design decisions (number of pads, stands, throughput tiers), and deterministic per-unit capacity overestimates real throughput due to queueing from stochastic service times.

Tiered Facility Selection with Closure,.definition: Introduce binary y_{j,t} (or ω_{i,s}) with Σ_t y_{j,t} ≤ 1 (or =1 if closure is a tier). Capacity = Σ_t cap_t·y_{j,t}, fixed cost = Σ_t cost_t·y_{j,t}. Services s are allowed only for tiers that include them via z_s ≤ Σ_{t∈T_s} y_{j,t}. For closure, tier 0 provides zero capacity and zero cost; when selected, flow variables are forced to zero because positive-tier multipliers vanish. In multi-period settings, enfor...
Tiered Facility Selection with Closure,.condition: When a facility can be opened at one of several discrete tiers that define capacity, service eligibility, and cost, possibly including a closure state and expansions over time.

Multi-Echelon Facility Role Assignment.definition: Assign each site a type indicator (e.g., H, P, S) with binary variables. Only allow flow on arcs that respect the hierarchy (e.g., H↔P, P↔S, H↔H, P↔P; forbid H↔S). Predefine allowed adjacency matrix and restrict flow variables to those arcs.
Multi-Echelon Facility Role Assignment.condition: When designing a hub-and-spoke network with three distinct facility types (aggregation, transfer, last-mile) and shipments must be routed through a transfer point before reaching a last-mile point.

Bilevel Network Design with Congestion E.definition: Evaluate each infrastructure decision together with the resulting user equilibrium. Allowing the planner to assign all flows directly can produce a system-optimal allocation that users would not select. A bilevel formulation preserves the dependence of route choice on infrastructure and congestion. With fixed origin–destination demand, separable, continuous, nondecreasing link costs, and standard flow-conservation constraints, the equilibrium can be represented by the traffic-assignment problem below. A KKT reformulation additionally requires the relevant regularity conditions.
Bilevel Network Design with Congestion E.condition: This principle applies when a planner selects infrastructure in a congestible network, while users independently choose routes according to their travel costs. Infrastructure decisions must affect the feasible routes or their congestion costs.

Logit Choice with Queueing-Derived Utili.definition:
In UAM network design, passenger demand should be modeled as endogenous when operational decisions influence service quality. For each OD pair $od$, the UAM utility can include
$$
  U_{od}^{\mathrm{UAM}}=-\alpha P_{od}-\beta\bigl(T_{\mathrm{flight},od}+W_k\bigr),
$$
where $P_{od}$ is the ticket price, $T_{\mathrm{flight},od}$ the flight time, and $W_k$ the expected queueing delay at vertiport $k$. The waiting time is obtained from a queueing model, such as $M/D/n$,
$$
  W_k=f(\lambda_k,\mu_k,n_k),
$$
where $\lambda_k$ is the passenger arrival rate, $\mu_k$ the service rate, and $n_k$ the number of service resources. Demand capture is then
$$
  D_{od}^{\mathrm{UAM}}
  =D_{od}\,\frac{\exp\bigl(U_{od}^{\mathrm{UAM}}\bigr)}
  {\exp\bigl(U_{od}^{\mathrm{UAM}}\bigr)+\exp\bigl(U_{od}^{\mathrm{ground}}\bigr)}.
$$
This creates the coupling facility decisions $\to$ queue delay $\to$ utility $\to$ UAM demand. Therefore, vertiport capacity and fleet decisions cannot be optimized independently from demand. If queueing delay is ignored, the model may overestimate demand because it assumes unlimited service capacity and neglects congestion-induced disutility.
Logit Choice with Queueing-Derived Utili.condition: When UAM demand is not fixed but depends on passenger mode choice, and the perceived utility of UAM includes endogenous service attributes such as vertiport waiting time, which is determined by fleet size, landing pads, chargers, or scheduling decisions.

Two-Stage Stochastic Facility Location.definition: Use a two-stage stochastic program: first-stage binary location decisions; second-stage per-scenario demand allocation variables, minimizing expected operational cost plus penalty for unmet demand. Standard stochastic facility location pattern.
Two-Stage Stochastic Facility Location.condition: When facility locations must be chosen under demand uncertainty, represented by a finite set of discrete scenarios with probabilities.

Altitude-Energy and Density Optimization.definition: Model sortie energy as a function of hub height h: ascent energy proportional to max(0, z_c - h), plus hover and horizontal. Density field analysis shows that higher h reduces peak density. Formulate objective (energy or time) with h as decision variable, and enforce local density constraint max_{x,y,z} ρ ≤ ρ_safe.
Altitude-Energy and Density Optimization.condition: When an airborne fulfillment center can hover at a variable altitude and drones perform deliveries, and energy consumption/airspace density depend strongly on hub height, with a safety limit on peak drone density.

Facility Grid Capacity Coupling.definition: Introduce binary y_j and continuous power limit P_j, with P_j ≤ M·y_j. Operational charging load per time interval must not exceed P_j. Include linear cost c_j P_j in objective.
Facility Grid Capacity Coupling.condition: When facility location decisions must also design electrical grid connection capacity, which limits the maximum total charging load at any time.

Demand Hub Alignment Verification.definition: Use a catchment radius for each hub: assign each demand trip's origin and destination to the nearest hub within the radius. Only include pairs where both ends are assigned. Compute the fraction of total demand covered; if coverage is low, expand candidate hubs or add ground access arcs to avoid biased flow volumes and suboptimal network designs.
Demand Hub Alignment Verification.condition: When demand is derived from mobile phone signaling data with precise coordinates and candidate hubs are discrete points, filtering OD pairs to only those where both origin and destination geocodes exactly coincide with hub locations can discard a large share of real trips, severely underestimating viable demand.

Node Capacity Constraints.definition: Build a time-expanded graph with layers t=1..T. Binary occupancy variables x_{f,s,t} for each flight f on segment s at t, and y_{f,p,t} for pad p. Arc capacity: sum_f x_{f,s,t} ≤ cap_s. Node capacity: sum_f (y_land_{f,v,t} + y_takeoff_{f,v,t}) ≤ pad_cap_v. Flight continuity via flow conservation across time. Turnaround blocking is enforced by prohibiting overlapping occupancy of a pad for the required turn duratio...
Node Capacity Constraints.condition: When flights must be scheduled through a network of corridors and vertiports over discrete time steps, and both corridor segments (arcs) and vertiport pads/nodes have limited capacity per time interval (occupancy slots, throughput limits). Optionally includes pad turnaround blocking.

Time-Expanded Slot Network.definition: Build a time-expanded graph with layers t=1..T. Binary occupancy variables x_{f,s,t} for each flight f on segment s at t, and y_{f,p,t} for pad p. Arc capacity: sum_f x_{f,s,t} ≤ cap_s. Node capacity: sum_f (y_land_{f,v,t} + y_takeoff_{f,v,t}) ≤ pad_cap_v. Flight continuity via flow conservation across time. Turnaround blocking is enforced by prohibiting overlapping occupancy of a pad for the required turn duratio...
Time-Expanded Slot Network.condition: When flights must be scheduled through a network of corridors and vertiports over discrete time steps, and both corridor segments (arcs) and vertiport pads/nodes have limited capacity per time interval (occupancy slots, throughput limits). Optionally includes pad turnaround blocking.

Arc Activation Constraints.definition: Introduce a binary parameter or variable z (arc-closure) or auth_{f,a} (flight‑specific approval). Constrain flow by f ≤ M · z or f_{f,a} ≤ M · auth_{f,a}. For weather/closures, z can be data‑driven (set to 0 when threshold exceeded); for authorization, auth is scenario‑dependent. This cleanly gates flow without altering the graph topology.
Arc Activation Constraints.condition: When corridor arcs or route segments have binary allowed/disallowed status due to external factors (weather closures, TFRs, NOTAMs) or regulatory authorization (e.g., LAANC), and flow must be by a Big‑M constraint so that disallowed arcs carry zero flow.

Authorization-Gated Arc Activation.definition: Introduce a binary parameter or variable z (arc-closure) or auth_{f,a} (flight‑specific approval). Constrain flow by f ≤ M · z or f_{f,a} ≤ M · auth_{f,a}. For weather/closures, z can be data‑driven (set to 0 when threshold exceeded); for authorization, auth is scenario‑dependent. This cleanly gates flow without altering the graph topology.
Authorization-Gated Arc Activation.condition: When corridor arcs or route segments have binary allowed/disallowed status due to external factors (weather closures, TFRs, NOTAMs) or regulatory authorization (e.g., LAANC), and flow must be by a Big‑M constraint so that disallowed arcs carry zero flow.

Geofence Arc Exclusion.definition: Overlay candidate arcs with geofence polygon boundaries. For each arc (i,j), if the segment intersects any geofence, either remove the arc from the graph or fix its capacity to zero. This guarantees no flight can cross a geofence without adding in‑model constraints.
Geofence Arc Exclusion.condition: When the spatial network must avoid predefined geofence polygons and any arc whose line segment intersects a geofence is infeasible. Use preprocessing to exclude non‑conformant arcs.

Noise Budget Constraint.definition: Add a linear constraint summing noise contributions over arcs used by non‑exempt flights: ∑_{a∈A_noise} n_a · (flow from non‑exempt flights on a) ≤ noise_limit. Exempt flights are omitted from the sum, so they can operate even when the budget is exhausted.
Noise Budget Constraint.condition: When a cumulative noise limit (e.g., Lden budget) applies across an area, flights contribute known noise per arc, and certain flight categories (medevac) may be exempt from the budget.

Noise Budget with Category Exclusions.definition: Add a linear constraint summing noise contributions over arcs used by non‑exempt flights: ∑_{a∈A_noise} n_a · (flow from non‑exempt flights on a) ≤ noise_limit. Exempt flights are omitted from the sum, so they can operate even when the budget is exhausted.
Noise Budget with Category Exclusions.condition: When a cumulative noise limit (e.g., Lden budget) applies across an area, flights contribute known noise per arc, and certain flight categories (medevac) may be exempt from the budget.

Layered Altitude Network Flow.definition: Model the network as a set of altitude-layer subgraphs. Each subgraph contains nodes and horizontal arcs with per‑arc capacity. Vertical arcs connect corresponding nodes in adjacent layers, incurring a transition cost. This captures spatial separation and vertical off‑loading within a single unified flow graph, supporting MIP or shortest‑path formulations.
Layered Altitude Network Flow.condition: The planning domain involves navigation in a 3D space that is naturally layered (e.g., altitude bands), and congestion in one layer can be bypassed by switching to another layer via vertical arcs.

Fluid Throughput Flow Approximation.definition: Use continuous flow variables f_{uv} (packages per hour) on arcs. Enforce flow conservation at each node and node processing throughput constraints. The resulting LP avoids integer variables and keeps facility location–allocation tractable at scale.
Fluid Throughput Flow Approximation.condition: High‑volume small‑package drone cargo (≤5 lb items, hundreds per hour) where discrete entity tracking is unnecessary.

Multi-Commodity Flow.definition: Define a variable flow[h,i,j] for each commodity h on arc (i,j). Arc capacity constraints sum over h: ∑_h flow[h,i,j] ≤ cap[i,j] couple the commodities. Each commodity independently satisfies flow conservation, and the objective minimizes total cost over all commodities and arcs.
Multi-Commodity Flow.condition: When multiple distinct flow types (e.g., vehicle priority classes, package categories) traverse a shared directed network, and each arc has a finite capacity that limits the total flow across all types.

Multi-Commodity Flow Conservation.definition: For each commodity, enforce flow conservation at every node: Σ_i f_{ij}^k + supply_{j}^k − demand_{j}^k = Σ_k f_{ji}^k. Total flow on any arc is bounded by shared capacity: Σ_k f_{ij}^k ≤ cap_{ij}. This embeds supply/demand directly in the balance equations, removes the need for separate source/sink nodes, and allows flow splitting across paths.
Multi-Commodity Flow Conservation.condition: When multiple commodities (origin–destination pairs) traverse a shared network with arc capacities and each commodity has external supply/demand at nodes.

Dummy Node for Supply-Demand Imbalance.definition: Add a dummy sink (unused supply) with zero‑cost arcs from all supply nodes, or add a dummy source (unmet demand) with high‑penalty arcs. This preserves total unimodularity and avoids side constraints that break the pure network structure.
Dummy Node for Supply-Demand Imbalance.condition: When total supply exceeds total demand in a pure network flow model and there is no penalty for unused supply; or unmet demand must be penalized. Exclude if excess supply is prohibited or must be explicitly tracked as inventory.

Node-Splitting for Arc Lower Bound Enfor.definition: Replace arc (i,j) with two arcs: (i,k) with capacity U−L and cost c, and (j,k) with capacity L and cost 0, where k is a new node. Adjust node supplies so that exactly L units are forced through the (j,k) arc, satisfying the lower bound without additional constraints.
Node-Splitting for Arc Lower Bound Enfor.condition: When a minimum‑cost flow problem includes a positive lower bound L_ij > 0 on an arc and the model must respect it while remaining a pure network problem (no explicit lower‑bound constraints). Exclude when L=0 or side constraints already exist.

Negative Cycle Detection for Unbounded M.definition: A directed cycle with total cost < 0 and no capacity limits allows infinite flow circulation, driving the objective to −∞. Diagnose by checking for negative‑cost cycles and add an upper bound on any arc in the cycle to cap the flow.
Negative Cycle Detection for Unbounded M.condition: When a min‑cost network flow LP with negative arc costs is unbounded and cycles are not explicitly bounded (no capacity or upper limits on recirculations). Exclude when all costs are non‑negative or arc capacities restrict cycle flow.

Flow-Dependent Arc Travel Cost (BPR).definition: Model the non‑linear congestion function via piecewise‑linear approximation using SOS2 constraints to keep the problem MILP‑solvable. For system‑optimum pricing, use marginal cost t(f) + f·t'(f). This captures both user‑equilibrium (UE) and system‑optimum (SO) routing, which differ whenever t'(f) > 0.
Flow-Dependent Arc Travel Cost (BPR).condition: When arc travel time or cost increases noticeably with flow due to congestion and can be captured by the BPR function t(f)=t₀(1+α(f/C)^β). Exclude when flows are well below capacity and constant cost suffices.

Discrete Facility Service Level Coupling.definition: Precompute for each OD pair (i,j) and service tier s the maximum flow ψ_ijs if origin i is at tier s. Use binary variables ω_is = 1 if i selects tier s. Link actual flow ψ_ij via precomputed bounds: ψ_ij ≤ Σ_s ψ_ijs ω_is + M(ω_i0+ω_j0) (and matching lower bound). Arc travel time τ_ij is made a linear function of the tier indicators, e.g., τ_ij = t_f + (1−ρ_i)(t_g−t_f) where ρ_i is selected by ω. This eliminates no...
Discrete Facility Service Level Coupling.condition: When network nodes (facilities) operate at discrete service levels that affect arc traversal times and the maximum flow that can be captured on origin–destination pairs, and the model must stay linear. Exclude if service level is continuous or does not influence times/flows.

Aggregate Externality Constraint via Arc.definition: Precompute a coefficient e_a for each arc (e.g., visibility‑weighted noise dB, casualty risk per flight). Add a linear constraint Σ_a e_a·f_a ≤ T, where T is the hard aggregate limit. This transforms geographically detailed safety or noise regulations into a simple flow constraint, avoiding expensive spatial simulation inside the optimisation.
Aggregate Externality Constraint via Arc.condition: When each unit of flow on an arc generates a fixed per‑unit externality (noise, ground risk) that must be constrained in aggregate, and per‑arc coefficients can be precomputed from spatial data. Exclude if externalities are non‑linear or depend on arc interactions.

Resource Ratio Coupling.definition: Model as cross-pool coupling: total active aircraft ≤ Σ_c ratio_c × pilots_active_in_category_c. With a single automation level, this simplifies to Σ active ≤ ratio × active_pilots. This directly links flight schedule variables to crew resource variables, preventing schedules that exceed pilot monitoring capacity.
Resource Ratio Coupling.condition: Trigger when fleet size is limited by remote-pilot headcount through known automation levels (e.g., HOVTL, HOTL, HWTL), possibly with pilots assigned to distinct categories. Exclude when each vehicle requires a dedicated operator with no automation or categories.

Eligibility-Constrained Assignment.definition: Pre-screen pairs: build an eligibility matrix M_{v,m} = 1 if vehicle v meets all hard requirements. Define assignment variables only for eligible pairs; fix all other combinations to zero or omit them entirely. This eliminates infeasible assignments, enforces compliance, and reduces model size.
Eligibility-Constrained Assignment.condition: Triggered when missions, facilities, or tasks have restrictions (regulatory category, payload/range, health, infrastructure type, VTOL capability) that render certain vehicle types ineligible. Exclude when all vehicles can serve all tasks.

Multi-Resource Crew Bundle.definition: Cap the number of active vehicles of each type by the most limiting resource: Z_type ≤ floor(available_roles / required_per_vehicle) for each role. This is a set of simple linear bounds that ensures no mission type activates more vehicles than any single crew pool can support, without per-vehicle binary assignment.
Multi-Resource Crew Bundle.condition: Mission types each require a fixed number of specialists (pilots, nurses, paramedics, etc.) per concurrently active vehicle, and these personnel pools have finite sizes.

Concurrent Task Limit (Fixed Cardinality.definition: Introduce binary variable c_{v,t} = 1 if vehicle v uses the resource at time t. Enforce Σ_v c_{v,t} ≤ C_max for every time slot. This captures the physical limitation that only C_max high‑voltage connections can be energized concurrently, which may be stricter than an aggregate energy budget.
Concurrent Task Limit (Fixed Cardinality.condition: Apply when infrastructure enforces a hard limit on simultaneous occupancy (e.g., fire‑safety rules limit concurrent fast-charging events to C_max), independent of fleet size or average throughput.

Cycle-Time Derived Service Capacity.definition: Compute maximum trips per resource: T_max = floor(operational_minutes / cycle_minutes). Constrain total assignments to that resource: Σ_f assign_{f,r} ≤ T_max. This directly ties resource count to achievable throughput without scheduling each minute.
Cycle-Time Derived Service Capacity.condition: Relevant when each use of a pad/station has a deterministic cycle time (flight + recharge + turnaround) and all operations must fit within a fixed daily window; use when time windows are well defined.

Coverage Slack Variables.definition: For each coverage constraint, add a nonnegative slack variable s_s on the supply-constrained side: Σ x + s = demand. Penalize sum of slacks in the objective. This transforms a potentially infeasible problem into a feasible one while minimizing shortfalls. The slack directly measures unmet demand.
Coverage Slack Variables.condition: Total supply of workers/vehicles may be unable to cover all demand; under-coverage is tolerated but must be penalized. Use when the problem would otherwise be infeasible.

Dual-Variable Capacity Pricing and Expan.definition: Optimal dual variables give the marginal value of one more unit of capacity. For pricing, set usage fee equal to the dual. For time‑varying slots, the per‑slot dual π_t indicates the optimal time-of-day pricing. For expansion, rank constraints by dual value and cross-check allowable increase to ensure the dual remains valid for the planned increment. In degenerate cases, the subgradient interval [p_min, p_max] yie...
Dual-Variable Capacity Pricing and Expan.condition: When an LP solves a resource‑allocation model and marginal values of capacity constraints (vertiport slots, airspace segments, production resources) are required for slot pricing, bottleneck ranking, or expansion planning. Include cases of primal degeneracy with multiple dual solutions, and use sensitivity analysis (allowable increase) to validate expansi...

Lifetime-Window Availability Summation.definition: Define C_t = Σ_{τ=t-L+1}^{t} x_τ, where x_τ is capacity added in year τ. This linear aggregation directly links earlier decisions to later capacity without tracking individual retirements. Apply to any resource with a fixed validity window.
Lifetime-Window Availability Summation.condition: Capacity additions have a known finite lifetime L (e.g., equipment, permits, carbon credits). Total available capacity in each year t is the sum of additions made in the most recent L years.

Proportional Resource Cap.definition: Express as a linear inequality: Σ_{i∈A} cap_i ≤ φ · Σ_{j∈All} cap_j. Because the total appears on both sides, it remains linear. This scales to any number of resource types and is directly implementable in LP/MIP.
Proportional Resource Cap.condition: A constraint mandates that a certain resource type (e.g., nuclear, renewables) must not exceed a fraction φ of total capacity, where both are sums of decision variables.

Battery Weight-Payload Coupling.definition: Linear coupling: payload_mass ≤ MTOM − (empty_mass + weight_per_kWh × B). This directly links the energy and payload subsystems, ensuring that missions with heavier packages limit battery size, and long-range missions reduce carrying capacity.
Battery Weight-Payload Coupling.condition: When battery capacity is a decision variable and increasing it reduces available payload because of the battery's weight.

Repositioning Flow Variables.definition: Add decision variables for empty vehicle flows on each arc alongside passenger flows, and enforce node flow conservation including both types. The objective includes a repositioning cost term to prevent unnecessary empty moves while ensuring vehicles can move from surplus to deficit nodes.
Repositioning Flow Variables.condition: Applies when demand-responsive fleets require empty repositioning moves to balance asymmetric demand, and repositioning incurs measurable cost; exclude when repositioning is negligible or supply is static.

Queueing Fleet Size Constraint.definition: Use queuing approximations (M/M/1, M/D/n, or Adelman linearizations) to compute expected queue length at each station as a function of utilization or flow. The total fleet required equals the sum of expected queue lengths plus vehicles in transit, converting operational waiting time into a hard capacity constraint on fleet size.
Queueing Fleet Size Constraint.condition: When fleet size is a decision variable and waiting times or service level requirements impose a limit on queue length; covers open and closed queueing networks. Exclude when fleet size is fixed or queueing is irrelevant.

Fairness-Acceptance Pricing Penalty.definition: Introduce a penalty term in the objective (e.g., quadratic or piecewise-linear) that grows with |p_ij − p_ref|. This captures fairness concerns and prevents extreme price variation while still allowing demand steering.
Fairness-Acceptance Pricing Penalty.condition: When demand can be shifted via pricing but large price deviations degrade passenger willingness; incorporate dissatisfaction as a convex penalty on deviation from reference price.

Mutually Exclusive Technology Alternativ.definition: Embed the choice via binary variables that switch parameter sets. Linear expressions for emissions, costs, payload capacity, and energy consumption are formed as sums over technologies of (parameter × binary). This enables simultaneous optimization of fleet composition and operation.
Mutually Exclusive Technology Alternativ.condition: The emission factor and performance parameters differ substantially between technology options (e.g., fuel cells 3.5× lower emission factor than Li‑ion) and the technology choice is a decision variable.

Stochastic & Robust Formulations.definition: First stage selects a buffer capacity for each site; second stage assigns emergency flights to the reserved capacity, with a heavy penalty for unmet missions. Regular throughput is capped at total capacity minus the buffer. This yields a two‑stage stochastic integer program balancing investment in buffers against expected penalty.
Stochastic & Robust Formulations.condition: When high‑priority stochastic demand (e.g., medevac, emergency flights) can preempt low‑priority operations and a minimum service level must be guaranteed by reserving dedicated capacity (pads, chargers, slots) at each facility. Exclude when priority demand is deterministic or can be absorbed by flexible re‑scheduling without dedicated buffers.

Selection.definition: A greedy algorithm that sequentially picks the element with largest marginal increase in the submodular function provides a tight (1‑1/e) lower bound. This solution can initialize a MIP start or be used as a stand‑alone heuristic for large instances. The submodular property guarantees that the final objective is never worse than this factor of optimal.
Selection.condition: When the problem involves location or coverage with diminishing returns (overlapping coverage, redundant sensors) and a cardinality budget limits the number of selected items. Exclude if synergy or supermodular effects exist.

Mission Energy.definition: Ignoring propulsion energy leads to solutions that prescribe excessive hovering or long flight paths, which are infeasible in practice because flight/hovering energy is orders of magnitude greater than communication energy. The model must jointly optimize flight trajectory and transmission power to achieve a realistic minimum-energy strategy.
Mission Energy.condition: When planning UAV communication relay trajectories or hovering positions, always include propulsion energy alongside transmission power in the objective or constraints. Exclude when transmission power dominates (e.g., very high-power transmitters) or flight is negligible (tethered drone).

Cumulative Risk Constraint (Exposure Lim.definition: Introduce a linear constraint per vehicle: ∑_{a∈path} r_a · x_a ≤ R_max, with r_a the risk on arc a and x_a a binary arc traversal variable. If candidate route sets are enumerated, sum risk over selected arcs. This enforces aggregate exposure limits without non-linear risk accumulation models.
Cumulative Risk Constraint (Exposure Lim.condition: When path planning must respect a cumulative safety risk budget, e.g., ground-impact fatality risk, using a discretized risk mask over the environment.

Sensor Coverage Feasibility Constraint.definition: Pre-process candidate arcs: compute required safe lookahead distance d_safe(v) based on current speed v, and compare with the sensor’s coverage radius R_sensor. If R_sensor < d_safe(v), arcs where that speed is needed are made infeasible. Alternatively, add a constraint that forces speed_v ≤ v_max where coverage is sufficient, coupling velocity profile decisions with sensor capability.
Sensor Coverage Feasibility Constraint.condition: Small UAS with limited onboard detect-and-avoid must guarantee that at every point along the planned route the distance to the nearest unsensed obstacle that could be encountered exceeds the kinematic reaction and braking distance.

Multimodal Ground Movement Choice.definition: Model each required ground leg as a set of parallel dummy arcs from origin to destination. For movement m, define binary x_{m,k} for each mode k and constraint sum_k x_{m,k} = 1. The travel time is sum_k (dist_m/speed_k) * x_{m,k}, and energy consumed is sum_k (energy_per_meter_k * dist_m) * x_{m,k}. This links mode choice to schedule delay and battery usage, enabling optimization of taxi operations.
Multimodal Ground Movement Choice.condition: Ground vehicles can use multiple taxi modes (e.g., hover at 3.25 m/s, passive tow at 2.63 m/s, active wheel at 2.15 m/s) with known speed and energy consumption per mode. The selected mode determines travel time and energy cost for each ground leg.

Headway-Augmented Edge Cost.definition: For each arc, maintain a list of occupancy intervals. When planning a new vehicle, if its traversal would overlap or follow another within the required headway Tg, the effective cost of that arc becomes base travel time + Tg. This naturally spaces out flights without binary sequencing variables. It yields a congestion‑aware cost function suitable for tactical rerouting or real‑time digital twin.
Headway-Augmented Edge Cost.condition: Used in A*/Dijkstra or similar search where paths are planned sequentially for multiple vehicles, knowledge of previous bookings on edges is available, and adding a gap time is preferred over a disjunctive scheduling model.

Subtour Elimination Constraints.definition: SEC forces for any subset S of nodes not containing depot, sum of edges crossing the cut is at least 2 (or at least 1 for directed). This formulation provides a stronger LP relaxation than MTZ's big-M time constraints. In practice, add SEC lazy cuts via callback when integer solutions contain subtours; the master LP remains compact.
Subtour Elimination Constraints.condition: When solving vehicle routing or TSP models where LP relaxation strength is critical, use cutset subtour elimination (SEC) inequalities rather than Miller–Tucker–Zemlin (MTZ) lifted constraints, as SEC yields a tighter LP bound. MTZ is acceptable for small instances or when callback separation is unavailable.

Arc Time Propagation (Big-M).definition: The constraint τ_j ≥ τ_i + s_i + t_ij − M(1−δ_ij), with M sufficiently large (e.g., horizon end), ensures that if δ_ij = 1 then τ_j ≥ τ_i + s_i + t_ij, propagating time along the route; if δ_ij = 0 the inequality is relaxed. This is essential for VRP with time windows, replacing MTZ constraints. Use careful choice of M to avoid weak LP bounds.
Arc Time Propagation (Big-M).condition: When a routing model uses binary arc variables δ_ij to decide whether a vehicle travels from i to j, and arrival times at nodes must respect travel times and service durations, but time propagation should only be enforced if the arc is selected.

Vehicle Rendezvous Synchronization (Stop.definition: Introduce continuous variables for truck arrival τ_arr_i and departure τ_dep_i at each stop i. Drone launch time t_launch ≥ τ_arr_i + prep; recovery time t_recov ≤ τ_dep_j (if recovering at same or another stop). Add battery constraints: total flight time ≤ max endurance. If binary stop selection variables are used, linearize via Big‑M linking. This couples truck and drone schedules via shared stop times.
Vehicle Rendezvous Synchronization (Stop.condition: When trucks act as drone bases and drones must launch and recover only at truck stops, with battery endurance and time window constraints. Exclude if moving recovery is required.

Mobile Arc-Based Drone Recovery Synchron.definition: Model each truck arc (i,j) with travel time T. Drone launch at t_launch, and recovery at t_return = t_start + αT, where α ∈ [0,1] is either a decision variable (optimized meeting point) or a fixed fraction. The drone sortie time equals αT − launch lag. Battery and payload constraints must hold for the sortie. This couples truck progress and drone flight; linearize by discretizing α or using continuous variable wit...
Mobile Arc-Based Drone Recovery Synchron.condition: Use when the truck route includes moving recovery; i.e., the truck can rendezvous with a drone while driving and the recovery location is a variable fraction along an arc. Exclude if retrieval always occurs at fixed stops. Requires known truck speed, drone speed, and travel time along each arc.

Multi-Drop Drone Sortie with Payload-Wei.definition: Define the drone sortie as a TSP/VRP path starting and ending at truck stops. Track cumulative payload after each delivery: load after node i = previous load − demand_i, kept nonnegative. Energy consumption on arc (i,j) = (α + β·load_{ij})·dist_ij, coupling routing, payload, and range. Battery balance: soc_j = soc_i − e_{ij} ≥ reserve. Add subtour elimination and time windows as needed. This yields sequence‑depend...
Multi-Drop Drone Sortie with Payload-Wei.condition: Use when drone capacity permits multiple deliveries per flight and deliveries can be sequenced, and payload-sensitive energy consumption must be modeled. Exclude when the drone carries only a single parcel per sortie (constant payload), simplifying to point‑to‑point energy.

Speed Ratio Gate for Drone Viability.definition: If drone speed is less than twice the truck’s speed, the drone’s flight plus synchronization delays (launch, recovery, handover) often exceed the time a truck would take to serve the same customer. Applying this gate reduces variable count and prevents the model from wasting computation on marginally beneficial drone sorties. Implement as a filter when generating feasible truck‑drone arcs.
Speed Ratio Gate for Drone Viability.condition: Apply as a data pre‑processing rule before constructing the optimization model: when truck and drone speeds are known, remove drone arcs or drone‑truck combinations where drone_speed < 2 × truck_speed. Exclude if non‑time objectives dominate (CO₂, cost) or drone availability is abundant.

Candidate Waypoint Coverage Constraint.definition: Precompute per‑target feasible waypoint sets. Introduce binary visit variables for waypoints. Add constraints ∑_{p∈S_i} visit_p ≥ 1 (set covering) or = 1 (set partitioning). This transforms spatial coverage or quality requirements into standard routing constraints, avoiding complex area coverage or sensor accuracy models inside the MILP.
Candidate Waypoint Coverage Constraint.condition: When each target (zone or inspection point) must be covered by the UAV visiting at least one (or exactly one) representative point from a precomputed set of feasible waypoints (e.g., zones with equivalent points, or viewpoints meeting an accuracy threshold).

Arc Energy Multi-Factor Modeling.definition: Model per‑arc energy as e = d · f(Δh, speed, payload) where f is a linear or piecewise‑linear function. Use SOS2 constraints to linearize if needed. This couples route geometry and payload/speed decisions with battery/hydrogen capacity constraints, enabling accurate energy‑aware routing.
Arc Energy Multi-Factor Modeling.condition: When UAV energy consumption is affected by altitude change, speed, payload, or power source characteristics and must be accounted for in routing.

Turn-Cost Sequence Dependency.definition: Model by augmenting nodes with approach heading, turning edge costs into asymmetric TSP with turn penalties, or pre‑compute heading‑dependent costs with heuristics.
Turn-Cost Sequence Dependency.condition: When a vehicle has a minimum turn radius (Dubins vehicle) and edge costs depend on incoming heading, making path cost sequence‑dependent.

Processing-Time Dominance Routing Simpli.definition: Treat each task as a job with processing time equal to service duration; assign jobs to vehicles as a parallel‑machine scheduling problem, omitting spatial routing variables or adding a small constant overhead. This drastically simplifies the model.
Processing-Time Dominance Routing Simpli.condition: When vehicle service/charging/handling times dominate travel times (e.g., minutes vs seconds).

Disjunctive Temporal Separation Constrai.definition: Introduce a binary precedence variable y_{ij} for each pair. Enforce mutual exclusion of order via y_{ij} + y_{ji} = 1 (if both use the segment), and disjunctive Big‑M constraints: t_j ≥ t_i + headway − M(1−y_{ij}), t_i ≥ t_j + headway − M·y_{ij}, with M = scheduling horizon. This lets a MIP solver select a conflict‑free sequence without pre‑enumerating all orders.
Disjunctive Temporal Separation Constrai.condition: When multiple mobile agents (aircraft, UAVs) share a one-way corridor segment and must maintain a minimum temporal headway to avoid conflicts; continuous-time scheduling with no overtaking.

Resource-Constrained Turnaround Scheduli.definition: Formulate as a resource‑constrained project scheduling problem (RCPSP) with time‑indexed binary variables x_{v,r,t}=1 if vehicle v starts a task on resource r at time t. Enforce precedence (e.g., charging after arrival) and cumulative capacity: at any time slot, sum of tasks occupying resource r ≤ capacity_r. The schedule must fit between arrival and departure.
Resource-Constrained Turnaround Scheduli.condition: When vertiport ground operations (charging, maintenance, passenger transfer) must be scheduled under limited numbers of chargers, bays, and personnel, with the goal of minimizing turnaround time or maximizing throughput.

Endurance-Driven Deadline and Priority O.definition: Compute a hard deadline from remaining endurance: t_departure ≤ t_arrival + (E_rem − E_min) / r. Additionally, introduce a binary flag c_i = 1 if endurance ≤ reserve_threshold or delay ≥ limit. For any conflicting pair (i,j) on a shared resource, if c_i=1 and c_j=0, force precedence i before j. This couples energy limits with scheduling decisions, preventing endurance exhaustion and service‑level violations.
Endurance-Driven Deadline and Priority O.condition: When a vehicle has limited battery/fuel endurance and any holding or taxiing consumes this budget, making prolonged delay infeasible; also, when endurance or accumulated delay reaches a critical threshold, the vehicle must receive top scheduling priority.

Sequence-Dependent Separation Times.definition: Replace a constant headway with a lookup into a type‑dependent separation matrix S[type_i][type_j]. Use binary ordering variables and Big‑M: start_j ≥ end_i + S_{type_i,type_j} − M(1−y_{ij}). This accurately captures safety or service intervals without worst‑case approximation, improving throughput.
Sequence-Dependent Separation Times.condition: When a shared resource (pad, station) processes tasks of different categories and the required temporal gap between consecutive tasks depends on the ordered pair of categories (e.g., wake turbulence classes, fuel types).

Simultaneous Resource Exclusion Constrai.definition: Introduce binary occupancy variables o_{r,t}=1 if resource r is occupied at time t. For each dependent pair (r,s), enforce o_{r,t} + o_{s,t} ≤ 1 for all time steps t. This mutual exclusion ensures safety compliance without detailed aerodynamic modeling.
Simultaneous Resource Exclusion Constrai.condition: When two or more spatial resources (pads, runways) are too close for simultaneous operations due to overlapping safety zones or wake turbulence, preventing concurrent usage.

Fixed Incumbent Occupancy Forbidden Inte.definition: Derive binary unavailability parameters o_{g,t} from the incumbent schedule. New service occupancy x_{i,g,t} is then bounded: x_{i,g,t} ≤ 1 − o_{g,t} during the occupancy interval. This avoids adding disjunctive constraints between the two systems.
Fixed Incumbent Occupancy Forbidden Inte.condition: When new mobility services must share gates or stands with conventional operations whose schedule is fixed and unchangeable, creating pre‑determined unavailability windows.

Charging Schedule Grid Limit.definition: Introduce binary connection variables z_{v,t}=1 if vehicle v is plugged in at time t, drawing known power p_v. Add aggregate constraint Σ_v p_v·z_{v,t} ≤ P_max ∀ t. This couples the scheduling of arrivals/departures with battery state-of‑charge and charger assignments, forcing joint optimization of flight and charging sequences.
Charging Schedule Grid Limit.condition: When multiple electric vehicles charge simultaneously at a vertiport whose electrical power supply is capped (e.g., 500 kW). Do not use if each charger has an isolated supply.

Indicator-Enforced Time Windows.definition: Replace Big‑M formulations with solver‑provided indicator constraints (e.g., Gurobi’s addGenConstrIndicator) to improve numerical stability and eliminate artificial bounds. The syntax (x == 1) >> (t >= a) directly links the binary assignment to the time window.
Indicator-Enforced Time Windows.condition: When a task’s start or arrival time must respect a time window only if a binary assignment variable equals 1, and Big‑M would introduce an unnecessarily large, loose bound.

Cumulative Resource Capacity Constraints.definition: Use discrete‑time binary occupancy x_{i,t}=1 if job i is active at t. Enforce Σ_i (demand_i · x_{i,t}) ≤ capacity for every time step t. This directly limits the peak load on the resource.
Cumulative Resource Capacity Constraints.condition: When multiple jobs or flights share a scarce resource with limited capacity at any time instant (e.g., airspace sector, number of chargers). Exclude if the resource has unlimited capacity.

Human Operator Cognitive Workload Constr.definition: Two complementary modeling patterns: (1) Attention‑budget: a state variable a_t bounded by [A_min, A_max], depletes with number of active UAVs, replenishes during breaks; constraints a_{t+1} = a_t − α·n_active_t + β·rest_t, a_t ≥ 0, and mandatory breaks after a maximum continuous period. (2) Task alternation: limit consecutive high‑demand tasks per operator via moving‑window constraints (e.g., at most K high‑deman...
Human Operator Cognitive Workload Constr.condition: When human operators supervise multiple UAVs and must not exceed cognitive limits: either by limiting continuous monitoring duration, or by avoiding prolonged sequences of high‑demand tasks.

Coverage Handover Continuity Constraint.definition: For sortie i with start s_i and end e_i, enforce e_i − s_i ≤ endurance, and for the subsequent sortie j, enforce s_j ≤ e_i − T_handover, where T_handover is the required overlap time. Embed in a scheduling MILP with ordering constraints to guarantee continuous coverage.
Coverage Handover Continuity Constraint.condition: When battery‑limited drones must maintain uninterrupted coverage of a stationary point/area, requiring seamless handover with minimum overlap between departing and arriving sorties. Exclude if intermittent coverage is acceptable.

Endogenous SoC-Driven Setup Times.definition: Couple flight energy consumption to the charging duration used in scheduling constraints. A change in route or payload can change arrival energy, charging time, and the earliest feasible start of the next assignment. A fixed turnaround parameter omits these dependencies. Express battery states as energy quantities, or convert state-of-charge fractions using battery capacity, so that the charging equation has consistent units. Under constant effective charging power, the energy deficit directly determines charging time.
Endogenous SoC-Driven Setup Times.condition: This principle applies when charging between consecutive vehicle assignments depends on the arrival state of charge, which is determined by the preceding flight. It excludes settings with a prescribed, state-independent charging duration.

Alternative Service Mode Selection (Char.definition: Introduce a binary mode variable z_i (1 if swap). Turnaround time becomes a linear combination: TAT_i = T_swap·z_i + ( (SoC_target − SoC_arrival)/P_charger )·(1−z_i). Departure SoC is e_dep = E_max·z_i + (e_arr + P_ch·t_chg)·(1−z_i). Couple with energy balance on the preceding flight leg to determine arrival SoC, and restrict swap only to equipped gates and compatible vehicle types.
Alternative Service Mode Selection (Char.condition: When a vehicle at a vertiport can choose between battery charging (time depends on SoC deficit) and battery swapping (fixed time, resets SoC to maximum). Exclude if only one mode exists.

Min-Max Deviation.definition: Introduce auxiliary variables maxVal and minVal representing the extreme group totals. Then either minimize `maxVal - minVal` as a fairness objective or enforce `maxVal - minVal ≤ tolerance` as a hard constraint. This captures worst-case imbalance in a linear way.
Min-Max Deviation.condition: When an optimization model must balance a workload or resource metric (delays, shifts, etc.) across multiple groups and equity is measured by the gap between the maximum and minimum group totals.

Load Balancing Constraints.definition: Add per-operator slot-usage limits: for each operator, segment, and time, enforce an upper bound (to prevent dominance) and a lower bound (to ensure fair share). This load-balances corridor access among operators directly, reflecting equity requirements.
Load Balancing Constraints.condition: When airspace operations require equitable capacity usage across multiple operators, preventing a single operator from dominating corridor capacity while also guaranteeing minimum access.

Time-Order Fairness Constraints.definition: Model order preservation with binary precedence variables y_{i,j} indicating whether flight i is served before j. For strict no-overtaking, enforce y_{i,j}=1 when original order requires it. For limited overtaking, constrain the sum of overtakes per operator.
Time-Order Fairness Constraints.condition: When fairness includes sequencing expectations (e.g., flights served in request order) and resource-leveling alone would cause unacceptable overtaking between operators.

Energy Balance Equations.definition: Model energy as a dynamic inventory. For each vehicle and each event step, define E_step as energy after the event. E_after_charge = E_before_charge + charge_amount, where charge_amount is a decision variable bounded by charging power and duration. E_after_flight = E_before_flight - consumption. Constraints: 0.2*E_max ≤ E ≤ 0.9*E_max. This ensures battery constraints are integrated into scheduling and routing deci...
Energy Balance Equations.condition: Vehicles rely on battery power with finite capacity, consume energy during taxi and flight, and can be recharged during turnaround. Feasibility requires that state of charge never drops below a safety threshold and stays below maximum capacity.

Facility-Location Lot-Sizing Formulation.definition: Use the facility‑location style formulation: binary setup variables x_j and continuous assignment variables w_{jk} (fraction of period k demand satisfied from period j production). Constraints: Σ_{j≤k} w_{jk}=1 and w_{jk} ≤ x_j. The constraint matrix is totally balanced; the LP relaxation yields integer w_{jk} without explicit integrality, providing the convex hull of the ULS polytope.
Facility-Location Lot-Sizing Formulation.condition: When modeling uncapacitated lot sizing or fixed-charge decisions (e.g., production, charging events) over discrete time periods with setup and holding costs, and no production capacity or storage limits break the zero-inventory property.

Alternative Bills-of-Materials Constrain.definition: Instead of a single production variable with aggregated resource consumption, create variables per variant, each consuming its own resource. This yields separate capacity constraints, reflecting true substitution and preventing the model from over-using one resource while ignoring the other. Total production is the sum of the variant variables.
Alternative Bills-of-Materials Constrain.condition: Applies when a product has multiple mutually substitutable input options (e.g., two memory board types) and each option consumes a different, limited resource; the product quantity can be split across variants. Exclude when components share identical resource requirements.

Knapsack Constraints.definition: This pattern maps directly to a knapsack model: binary variables represent project adoption, a single budget constraint limits total spending, and the objective maximizes total benefit (throughput, economic impact). Linking constraints to downstream flow variables ensure only upgraded facilities host charging.
Knapsack Constraints.condition: The problem requires choosing a subset of airside upgrade projects (e.g., charging stations, grid connections) under a fixed total capital budget, where each project incurs a known cost and delivers a quantifiable benefit. Only selected projects become available for subsequent operations.

Incompatible Items Splitting Constraint.definition: Enforce that no drone or vehicle carries two items of incompatible types simultaneously. This is done via pairwise exclusion constraints per vehicle or by limiting each vehicle to one item type using a type‑assignment binary and indicator constraints, ensuring realistic delivery planning for meal or hazardous material transport.
Incompatible Items Splitting Constraint.condition: When items are classified into incompatible types and each vehicle can only carry items of a single type or must not carry conflicting pairs.

Network-Flow Reformulation for Integrali.definition: Replacing stock variables with arc flows on a time‑expanded network (production arcs, inventory arcs between periods, demand sinks) produces a totally unimodular constraint matrix. The LP optimal basis will be integer, eliminating the need for integer variables and enabling fast primal simplex with spanning‑tree bases.
Network-Flow Reformulation for Integrali.condition: When a multi‑period inventory or production planning problem has linear holding/ production costs, no setup binaries, and integer demand; the resulting network flow LP automatically yields integer stock levels.

Nonlinear Function Handling.definition: Prefer solver native direct general constraints (addGenConstrNL, addGenConstrMax) for supported functions to avoid manual reformulation. When a MIP is needed or the solver lacks direct support, use solver-native PWL (addGenConstrPWL) instead of manual λ/SOS2. Check convexity: if the function is convex in the optimisation sense, PWL needs only SOS2 and solves as an LP; non-convex requires binary variables and becom...
Nonlinear Function Handling.condition: The model contains univariate nonlinear terms (exp, sin, x^k) or non-smooth functions (max/min/abs) that would make the problem non-convex, or it requires piecewise-linear approximation of a univariate function and a solver-native PWL construct is available. Exclude when manual SOS2 branching or custom cut separation is required.

When a MIP is needed or the solver lacks direct support, use solver-native PWL (addGenConstrPWL) instead of manual λ/SOS2. Exclude when manual SOS2 branching or custom cut separation is required.

For complex logical conditions, apply per-variable Big‑M tightening (use the tightest bound, e.g., arc capacity), deadband Big‑M for threshold indicators, and systematic CNF-to-MIP conversion. For regime-switching, introduce binary indicators with weighted-sum or Big‑M to activate regime-spe...
Big-M & Indicator Variables.condition: Constraints or objective components depend on logical conditions (if-then, either-or, at-least-k), discrete operating regimes, demand thresholds, or disjunctive convex regions, and the model is solved as a MIP. Exclude when continuous expressions lack finite upper/lower bounds.

Logical and Big-M Indicator Constraints.definition: Use solver indicator constraints (addGenConstrIndicator) for simple variable-gated linear constraints to avoid manual Big‑M. For complex logical conditions, apply per-variable Big‑M tightening (use the tightest bound, e.g., arc capacity), deadband Big‑M for threshold indicators, and systematic CNF-to-MIP conversion. For regime-switching, introduce binary indicators with weighted-sum or Big‑M to activate regime-specific bounds. For disjunctive regions (union of convex polyhedra), use binary selection variables (sum y_i=1) and Big‑M per disjunct. Demand-triggered activation links a binary to a threshold condition via constraints. This yields a single MIP that automatically selects the correct constraint set.

For disjunctions, use convex-hull variable splitting: copy continuous variables for each disjunct k (x = Σ x^k), enforce disjunct constraints only on x^k with its binary y^k (Σ y^k=1), yielding the tightest LP relaxation. For corridor...
Disaggregation Tightening for Fixed-Char.condition: Naive Big‑M or aggregated fixed-charge/disjunctive formulations produce a weak LP relaxation or an exponential number of constraints in time-indexed/disjunctive models, and tightening is needed. Exclude if the problem size becomes impractically large from disaggregation.
