For disjunctions, use convex-hull variable splitting: copy continuous variables for each disjunct k (x = Σ x^k), enforce disjunct constraints only on x^k with its binary y^k (Σ y^k=1), yielding the tightest LP relaxation. For corridor...
Strong Disjunctive and Separation Formul.condition: Naive Big‑M or aggregated fixed-charge/disjunctive formulations produce a weak LP relaxation or an exponential number of constraints in time-indexed/disjunctive models, and tightening is needed. Exclude if the problem size becomes impractically large from disaggregation.

Linearization of Non-linear Forms.definition: For two binaries x_i, x_j, introduce auxiliary continuous y_ij and enforce y_ij ≤ x_i, y_ij ≤ x_j, y_ij ≥ x_i + x_j − 1, y_ij ≥ 0. This exact linearization preserves 0‑1 integrality. For binary p times continuous s with upper bound D, enforce r ≤ P·s, P·s − r ≤ P·D·(1−p), and s ≤ D·p. This forces r = P·s when p=1 and r=0, s=0 when p=0, avoiding an auxiliary integer variable while keeping the model linear.
Linearization of Non-linear Forms.condition: The objective or constraints contain a product of two binary variables, or a product of a binary variable and a continuous variable that has a known natural upper bound (e.g., demand).

Product-of-Binary-and-Continuous Lineari.definition: For two binaries x_i, x_j, introduce auxiliary continuous y_ij and enforce y_ij ≤ x_i, y_ij ≤ x_j, y_ij ≥ x_i + x_j − 1, y_ij ≥ 0. This exact linearization preserves 0‑1 integrality. For binary p times continuous s with upper bound D, enforce r ≤ P·s, P·s − r ≤ P·D·(1−p), and s ≤ D·p. This forces r = P·s when p=1 and r=0, s=0 when p=0, avoiding an auxiliary integer variable while keeping the model linear.
Product-of-Binary-and-Continuous Lineari.condition: The objective or constraints contain a product of two binary variables, or a product of a binary variable and a continuous variable that has a known natural upper bound (e.g., demand).

Infeasibility Repair.definition: Add non‑negative slack/surplus variables to constraints. Optionally compute an Irreducible Inconsistent Subsystem (IIS) to identify the minimal conflicting set, then add slacks only to those. Minimize total weighted slack to obtain the smallest violation that restores feasibility. Solver utilities such as feasRelax automate the process. After repairing, re‑optimize with the original objective.
Infeasibility Repair.condition: Model is infeasible due to conflicting constraints and a feasible relaxation is required for diagnosis or as a starting point; infeasibility is not caused by trivial data errors.

Piecewise Step-Function Cost.definition: Use ordered binary variables b_k with precedence b_{k+1} ≤ b_k. Cumulative capacity = Σ Δcap_k · b_k, total cost = Σ Δcost_k · b_k. This gives an integer‑linear formulation without SOS2 constraints, enforcing that higher tiers are only available after lower tiers are installed.
Piecewise Step-Function Cost.condition: Infrastructure capacity expansion cost is a step function where each incremental block has a fixed size and cost, and blocks must be activated in sequence (e.g., grid upgrade tiers). Do not use for smooth cost curves better handled by SOS2 PWL.

LP Sensitivity Re-optimization.definition: The current basis remains optimal over an interval where reduced costs stay nonnegative (cost case) or basic variables stay nonnegative (RHS case). Compute these intervals via the basis inverse and simple linear inequalities; at the boundary a reduced cost or basic variable hits zero, requiring one pivot to obtain the new basis. This provides warm‑start re‑optimization and yields the piecewise‑linear value functio...
LP Sensitivity Re-optimization.condition: An LP objective cost vector or right‑hand side depends linearly on a scalar parameter, or a single RHS/coefficient changes, and the previous optimal basis is available. Exclude if the basis was not saved or the change is not local.

Convex Piecewise-Linear Linearization.definition: For an objective term max_k(a_k·x+b_k), introduce auxiliary variable z and add constraints z ≥ a_k·x+b_k; minimize z. For |g(x)| use t ≥ g(x), t ≥ −g(x). For a constraint max_k(f_k(x)) ≤ h, simply enforce f_k(x) ≤ h for all k. This preserves convexity and avoids binary variables, keeping the model linear.
Convex Piecewise-Linear Linearization.condition: An objective or constraint contains a convex piecewise‑linear function formed by max of affine terms, absolute value, or absolute change, and a pure LP (no integer variables) is required. Exclude nonconvex functions or when max appears on the “greater than” side.

Avoid Exact MILP for Combinatorial Optim.definition: Direct MILP linearization of QAP adds n⁴ variables and constraints, blowing up memory and time. Time‑indexed MILP for RCPSP rarely solves exactly for non‑trivial instances. Discretizing a continuous coverage area into a grid converts exact CPP into a combinatorial routing heuristic that may lose the true optimal continuous path. Instead, use specialized approaches: QAP‑specific heuristics/decomposition, priority‑r...
Avoid Exact MILP for Combinatorial Optim.condition: The problem is a quadratic assignment (n>10), resource-constrained project scheduling (>30 tasks), or continuous area coverage where exact optimality is required, and a direct MILP or grid-discretization leads to an intractable model (e.g., O(n⁴) variables for QAP, thousands of binaries for time‑indexed RCPSP) or loss of optimality (TSP grid heuristic for...

Symmetry Breaking Constraints.definition: Add a lexicographic ordering constraint on a monotonically assigned quantity (e.g., total demand served by agent k). Forcing that quantity to be non‑increasing across identical agents eliminates permutations without affecting feasibility, dramatically reducing the branch‑and‑bound search space.
Symmetry Breaking Constraints.condition: The model contains multiple identical entities (vehicles, machines, agents) whose assignment or routing variables create solution symmetry.

Domain-Specific Constraint Formulation.definition: Introduce a binary indicator z that activates when the decision variable crosses the threshold. Link via Big-M: var ≤ threshold − ε + M·z and var ≥ threshold·z (or var ≤ threshold−1+M·z for integer vars). Then use z to Big-M-activate the appropriate regulatory constraints. This avoids solving separate models per regime and correctly captures decision-dependent compliance costs.
Domain-Specific Constraint Formulation.condition: When a decision variable (e.g., weekly roundtrips, annual enplanements) crosses a statutory threshold that reclassifies the operation under a different regulatory part with distinct constraint blocks. Exclude when the regime is purely an external scenario parameter.

Domain Decomposition Strategy.definition: Decompose into a master problem that selects truck stop locations (and possibly a truck route) and a subproblem that checks drone delivery feasibility. With fixed stops, the drone subproblem becomes a convex assignment or network‑flow problem, enabling efficient solution and generation of strong optimality/feasibility cuts for the master.
Domain Decomposition Strategy.condition: When a truck-drone routing problem couples ground vehicle stops and drone sorties, and the integrated MIP is intractable. The truck acts as a mobile depot, drones serve nearby customers under range and payload limits. Exclude when drone range is not limiting.

Decomposition Strategy.definition: Each area solves a local scheduling/flow optimization that treats inbound/outbound boundary flows as decision variables subject to shared capacity quotas at CEPs. A federated coordinator or iterative negotiation protocol (priority rules, dual prices, proportional fairness) adjusts the quotas across areas to resolve conflicts and achieve global feasibility without sharing full internal demand data. This respects operational independence and avoids a monolithic solver.
Decomposition Strategy.condition: When the airspace can be partitioned into cooperative areas (different PSUs or separate domains) with known coordinated entry/exit points (CEPs), and a centralized monolithic optimization is infeasible or undesirable due to scale, privacy, or single-point-of-failure concerns. Not needed if the problem is small or areas are fully independent.

Perturbation Robustness Sensitivity Test.definition: For a formulation that may be ill‑conditioned, solve many times with tiny random perturbations (e.g., ±1e-6) added to objective coefficients and RHS. Track how often feasibility is lost and by how much the solution changes. If even tiny noise causes large solution jumps or infeasibility, the formulation is too sensitive and needs rescaling or constraint relaxation. Disabling presolve ensures the raw model behavior is tested.
Perturbation Robustness Sensitivity Test.condition: Applies when narrow separation margins (airspace corridors, energy limits) make the solution hypersensitive; exclude when problem is coarse and small perturbations cannot change feasibility.

MIP Optimality and Feasibility Caveat.definition: Never assume global optimality unless the solver returns OPTIMAL with zero gap. The incumbent is the best found; its objective may be far from the true optimum. Numerical instability can cause constraint slacks to be negative beyond the feasibility tolerance. Always verify critical constraints using actual variable values, and consider tightening tolerances or scaling coefficients.
MIP Optimality and Feasibility Caveat.condition: Applies whenever a MIP is terminated by a time limit or a non-zero MIP gap (status TIME_LIMIT or solution with positive gap), and when scaled-up instances risk floating-point violations.

Avoid Monolithic MILP for Integrated Tru.definition: Full MILP models with arc‑indexed variables, synchronization, and battery constraints become intractable beyond very small instances. Instead, decompose (e.g., master selects stops, subproblem solves drone routes) or use hybrid methods (Lin‑Kernighan heuristic + drone‑routing MILP). This prevents wasted effort on monolithic exact models.
Avoid Monolithic MILP for Integrated Tru.condition: When solving real‑world instances of Flying Sidekick, PDSTSP, or carrier‑vehicle problems where customer count exceeds roughly 10.

Optimization Solution Caveat.definition: The coupled PDE ∇·(κ(|∇φ|)∇φ)=q can have several solutions that satisfy the equilibrium condition. A standard Newton iteration with a fixed starting point may converge to a high‑cost local minimum. To avoid misleading results, verify optimality by re‑solving from several initial guesses, or use a global optimisation algorithm (multistart, genetic algorithm) when few design variables exist (e.g., barrier height).
Optimization Solution Caveat.condition: Applies whenever a continuum traffic equilibrium (Wardrop or system optimum) is solved via Newton’s method, and the underlying cost function or domain geometry makes the residual non‑convex, yielding multiple stable solutions.

Hierarchical/Epsilon-Constraint Multi-Ob.definition: Use either the solver's multi-objective API (e.g., Gurobi setObjectiveN with priority, ObjNRelTol/ObjNAbsTol) or a two‑phase manual epsilon‑constraint: Phase 1 optimize the primary objective to get best value p*, then impose primary ≤ p* + tolerance and optimize the secondary. The coverage‑energy trade‑off is a direct application of epsilon‑constraint (coverage ≥ α, min energy). This avoids numerical issues from h...
Hierarchical/Epsilon-Constraint Multi-Ob.condition: When the problem has multiple conflicting objectives with a priority order and you need to control degradation of higher-priority objectives (e.g., cost before fairness, coverage before energy), either via solver built-in multi-objective or manual epsilon-constraint.

Alternative Optima Handling.definition: Either preemptively add a tiny secondary penalty term (e.g., 1e‑6 * smoothness_cost) to the objective so the solver breaks ties automatically, or after solving the LP inspect non‑basic variables for zero reduced cost and binding constraints for zero shadow price to identify alternative optima and manually select a solution that improves secondary metrics.
Alternative Optima Handling.condition: When many distinct feasible solutions yield an identical optimal primary objective value, and a secondary criterion (smoothness, noise, etc.) is desired.

Priority-Weighted Tardiness/Recovery Obj.definition: Introduce non‑negative delay variables d_i ≥ completion_time_i − due_i, then minimize Σ w_i d_i. For recovery after a disruption, set the due time equal to the disruption instant and weight each task by its importance. This yields a linear objective that integrates seamlessly into any LP/MIP scheduling or assignment model.
Priority-Weighted Tardiness/Recovery Obj.condition: When tasks have due dates or a disruption occurs, and the objective is to minimize weighted delays or recovery duration, with task‑specific criticality weights.

Lifecycle Emission Objective with Techno.definition: Total emission = Σ (energy_consumed_kWh × ef_eff_tech) + Σ (vehicles × (ef_prod + ef_recycle)) + Σ (maintenance_hours × ef_maint). The effective emission factor per kWh is ef_eff = (ef_upstream + ef_direct)/η × (1 + deg). This prevents bias towards technologies with low direct but high upstream emissions and accounts for capacity fade in batteries.
Lifecycle Emission Objective with Techno.condition: When fleet composition and operation decisions must minimize total lifecycle carbon emissions, and technologies differ in upstream intensity, conversion efficiency, and degradation.

Competing Externality Trade-off.definition: Drone delivery displaces ground transport, reducing CO₂/NOx but adding noise. Model as a weighted‑sum objective: min α × noise_dose − β × emissions_saved, where noise dose is a spatially discretized sum over arcs and population zones, and emissions saved scale linearly with displaced distance. The ratio α/β defines the implied cost of noise vs. carbon.
Competing Externality Trade-off.condition: When modal substitution produces externalities with opposite signs and different units (e.g., noise vs. CO₂ savings), requiring an explicit multi‑objective treatment with a single trade‑off parameter.

Fractional Objective Binary Search.definition: Instead of nonlinear solvers, binary search over α is coupled with an LP that enforces the ratio inequality, linearizing the problem. Each iteration solves an LP feasibility instance; the final interval bounds the optimum to desired tolerance.
Fractional Objective Binary Search.condition: The model is a linear fractional program minimizing (or maximizing) a ratio of linear functions, the denominator sign is constant, and a fast LP solver is available.

Primary Cardinality Fix then Min-Max Bal.definition: Phase I solves min Σ δ_k. Phase II adds constraint Σ δ_k = K*, introduces continuous slack variables s_k ≥ 0 for each resource's limit L, enforces workload_k + s_k = L, and minimizes max s_k. This yields the best‑balanced schedule without increasing the minimal fleet size.
Primary Cardinality Fix then Min-Max Bal.condition: The first objective is minimizing the number of resources (binary sum), and after attaining the minimum, the goal is to balance workloads (time, capacity) across the used resources. Exclude if count and balance must be solved simultaneously with a single weighted sum.

Plan Instability Penalty (Rerouting Cost.definition: Introduce binary variables δ_i that equal 1 if the new assignment for item i differs from the baseline. Enforce with δ_i ≥ x_i − x̂_i and δ_i ≥ x̂_i − x_i (or Big‑M). Add penalty γ Σ δ_i to the objective. The penalty coefficient γ balances optimality and stability; source used this to limit the number of reroutings.
Plan Instability Penalty (Rerouting Cost.condition: Re‑optimization occurs online; each change to a previously communicated route/slot assignment incurs operational cost or degrades predictability. The objective must trade off current optimality against plan continuity.

Concave Reward from Repeated Independent.definition: If a target is visited k times, detection probability = 1−(1−p)^k, a concave function. A linear reward per visit would over‑value revisits. Reformulate the objective as a sum of piecewise‑linear concave segments per target, using binary variables to select the number of visits and SOS2 constraints to capture diminishing contributions.
Concave Reward from Repeated Independent.condition: The mission involves detecting stochastic targets where multiple independent passes increase detection probability (p known and constant per pass), and revisits yield diminishing returns.

Candidate Pre-Screening Elimination.definition: Apply a pre-filtering step to discard infeasible candidates, reducing the set for which binary decision variables are created. This shrinks the MIP size and avoids infeasibility from clearly unsuitable candidates.
Candidate Pre-Screening Elimination.condition: When many candidate sites/options exist and require pre-screening against readiness criteria (binary must-have checks, composite score thresholds, or spatial feasibility constraints) before optimization.

Total Unimodularity Preservation and Cau.definition: TU matrices allow continuous variable formulations to yield integer optimal solutions. Adding slacks or side constraints destroys TU, leading to fractional solutions; then original variables must be explicitly declared binary. Conversely, if TU structure can be preserved, solve as LP for speed.
Total Unimodularity Preservation and Cau.condition: When the problem's constraint matrix is (or would be) totally unimodular (e.g., assignment, network flow, cyclic scheduling with consecutive-ones interval matrix) and integer RHS, but slack variables or extra side constraints may be added.

Native Integer vs Binary Expansion.definition: Use native integer variables with bounds [0, U] instead of expanding into floor(log2(U))+1 binary variables. This keeps formulation compact and preserves stronger LP bounds.
Native Integer vs Binary Expansion.condition: When the problem intrinsically has integer variables (e.g., number of vehicles, trips) and not merely logical binary choices, and binary expansion would explode variable count and weaken LP relaxation.

Continuous vs Discrete Variable Selectio.definition: For large numbers of identical small items (e.g., parcels, flights), use continuous variables and round post-solve with negligible error. For large indivisible units (e.g., plants, large machines), use binary or integer variables to prevent fractional infeasibility.
Continuous vs Discrete Variable Selectio.condition: When modeling quantities where the choice exists between continuous and discrete variables, depending on the scale and indivisibility of items.

Unrestricted Variable Decomposition into.definition: Decompose free variable x into x⁺ − x⁻ with x⁺, x⁻ ≥ 0. At optimum, at most one is positive. This transformation is exact and enables standard-form solvers.
Unrestricted Variable Decomposition into.condition: When a decision variable is unrestricted in sign and the solver/algorithm requires nonnegative variables in standard form (min c^T x, Ax=b, x≥0).

Simple Bounds via Variable Attributes.definition: Set the bound directly as a variable attribute (e.g., x.UB = U) rather than adding a constraint. The reduced cost of x then directly gives the marginal value of relaxing the bound, providing cleaner sensitivity analysis.
Simple Bounds via Variable Attributes.condition: A variable has a simple upper/lower bound (e.g., x ≤ U) that is independent of other variables, and sensitivity information on the bound's value is desired.

Auxiliary Variable Integrality Relaxatio.definition: Keep w as a continuous variable; the constraints together with binary x,y force w to 0 or 1 at optimality, reducing the number of binary variables in the MIP.
Auxiliary Variable Integrality Relaxatio.condition: When linearizing products of binary variables (w = x·y) using auxiliary variable w and bounding constraints w ≤ x, w ≤ y, w ≥ x+y−1, and the objective function pushes w to its lower/upper bound.

Pattern Variable Reformulation for Symme.definition: Reformulate using pattern variables γ_k, the number of times pattern k is used. Master problem becomes set-partitioning/covering min Σ c_k γ_k subject to Σ_k a_jk γ_k ≥ 1 for each task, eliminating symmetry and enabling column generation.
Pattern Variable Reformulation for Symme.condition: When resources (vehicles, pipes, aircraft) are truly identical and interchangeable, leading to massive symmetry and equivalent solutions from per-unit assignment variables.

Closed-Form Optimal Elimination.definition: Solve dR/dh = 0 analytically for optimal h*, substitute into the model to eliminate the altitude variable, reducing variable count and avoiding nonlinearities while preserving optimality.
Closed-Form Optimal Elimination.condition: When a coverage metric (e.g., radio footprint radius) is a unimodal, differentiable function of a single continuous variable (e.g., altitude), and horizontal position is fixed or optimized separately.

Optimality Gap Calibration.definition: Relying solely on relative MIP gap may terminate with a large absolute gap if the objective is large (e.g., $1M objective, 0.01% relative = $100 absolute). Set MIPGapAbs to an application‑specific acceptable absolute error (e.g., $50) to guarantee practical precision.
Optimality Gap Calibration.condition: When objective magnitude is known and an absolute acceptable tolerance must be enforced.

Numerical Stabilization Strategy.definition: Combine aggressive scaling and numeric-focused solver settings with explicit finite bounds on all variables. ScaleFlag=2 applies row/column scaling; NumericFocus=1‑3 improves precision; MarkowitzTol near 0.999 avoids unstable LU pivots. Imposing large but finite bounds (e.g., ±1e6) on otherwise unbounded variables compacts the polyhedron, reduces aspect ratio, and prevents solution drift from tiny perturbations. A...
Numerical Stabilization Strategy.condition: When a Gurobi LP/MIP shows numerical instability signs (KappaExact > 1e12, coefficient range exceeding 1e9, ill‑conditioned basis warnings) OR contains continuous variables that could become unbounded or extremely large, making the feasible polyhedron thin and ill‑conditioned.

Multi-Scenario Feature (NumScenarios, Sc.definition: Set model.NumScenarios = K. For each scenario s, assign model.ScenNRhs[s, constr_name] = rhs_val, model.ScenNObj[s, var_name] = cost, etc. Gurobi builds the deterministic equivalent internally, sharing model structure. After optimization, access model.ScenNObjVal[s] for each scenario.
Multi-Scenario Feature (NumScenarios, Sc.condition: When demand/cost uncertainty is described by a small set of discrete scenarios, use Gurobi's NumScenarios, ScenNRhs, ScenNObj, ScenNUB to set scenario‑specific data without duplicating constraints, then retrieve scenario objective values.

Batch Coefficient Modification & Update.definition: Gurobi stores attributes lazily. Batch all modifications (lb, ub, obj, rhs) first, then call model.update() once before the next optimize. After optimization, use model.getAttr(attr, list) for bulk attribute retrieval. Always reference objects by handles, not numeric indices, to prevent index shift errors.
Batch Coefficient Modification & Update.condition: When using Gurobi and you need to query attributes before or after optimization, or when programmatically modifying many variable/constraint attributes between successive solves, to avoid stale values and per‑item overhead.

Lazy Model Update & Bulk Attribute Acces.definition: Gurobi stores attributes lazily. Batch all modifications (lb, ub, obj, rhs) first, then call model.update() once before the next optimize. After optimization, use model.getAttr(attr, list) for bulk attribute retrieval. Always reference objects by handles, not numeric indices, to prevent index shift errors.
Lazy Model Update & Bulk Attribute Acces.condition: When using Gurobi and you need to query attributes before or after optimization, or when programmatically modifying many variable/constraint attributes between successive solves, to avoid stale values and per‑item overhead.

Avoid reset() to Preserve Warm Start.definition: After modifying variable bounds or objective coefficients, simply call model.optimize() again. The solver (e.g., Gurobi) will detect that the abstract model is unchanged and will start from the previous basis. A call to model.reset() before optimize discards all warm‑start information, causing a cold start that can drastically increase solve time. Reset is only appropriate for completely independent major structur...
Avoid reset() to Preserve Warm Start.condition: Applies when you are re‑optimizing a model after small changes such as fixing some variables to integer values, changing right‑hand sides, or adding lazy constraints, and you want to benefit from a warm start. Avoid if the model structure changes dramatically.

Tupledict Wildcard Summation.definition: Use flow.sum('*', i, j) to sum over all commodities for a specific arc, flow.sum(h, '*', j) to sum over all incoming origins, and flow.sum(h, j, '*') to sum over all outgoing destinations. This replaces manual quicksum loops and reduces index‑related errors while keeping constraint expressions readable and efficient.
Tupledict Wildcard Summation.condition: When using Gurobi Python API and variables are stored in a tupledict (via addVars with multiple indices), and constraints require summing over one index dimension while keeping others fixed.

addVars with obj Argument.definition: Provide a dictionary mapping variable index tuples (e.g., (h,i,j)) to their unit costs as the obj argument of addVars. The solver automatically sets the variable's Obj attribute, so no separate setObjective or quicksum is needed. This reduces code duplication and the risk of mismatched objective terms.
addVars with obj Argument.condition: When every indexed variable has a predetermined cost coefficient and you are creating the variables with addVars on the same index sets.

Data Preparation with gp.multidict and g.definition: gp.multidict(dict_of_tuples) returns a tupledict (fast summation) and a flat list of keys. gp.tuplelist from the keys enables fast select('*', shift) or select(worker, '*') to iterate over allowed assignments without manual filtering. This reduces indexing errors and speeds model construction.
Data Preparation with gp.multidict and g.condition: When an optimization model has eligibility restrictions (e.g., worker‑shift availability) and data is provided as a dictionary of (key1, key2): value.

FeasRelax for Minimal Infeasibility Repa.definition: Call model.feasRelax(relaxobjtype=0, minrelax=False, ubpen=penalty_dict) to create a relaxed model where each constraint obtains a new slack/surplus variable and the objective minimizes the weighted L1 norm of those slacks. This directly yields a feasible solution with the cheapest violation, bypassing iterative IIS debugging. L2 introduces quadratic penalty requiring NonConvex=2 and slower solves; L0 gives unreli...
FeasRelax for Minimal Infeasibility Repa.condition: The initial MIP is infeasible because of hard constraints on deadlines, slot counts, or capacities; you need to identify a minimal relaxation that makes the model feasible, preferring automatic slack insertion over manual IIS analysis. Also, when choosing a penalty norm, use L1 to preserve model class and avoid quadratic non‑convexity.

Batch Model Submission for Many Instance.definition: Build a list of model objects, then use Gurobi's batch solve to dispatch them to a cluster manager. This avoids sequential solves and manual parallel loops, leveraging load balancing and efficient job scheduling.
Batch Model Submission for Many Instance.condition: The user needs to solve many independent optimization instances (100+) with identical variable and constraint structure but different coefficients, and parallel hardware is available.

Time-Limited IIS Completeness Check.definition: An approximate IIS from time‑limited computation may contain redundant constraints—it is not guaranteed irreducible. Before using the IIS to drive automatic repair (e.g., adding slacks only to IIS constraints), check each constraint's IISMinimal attribute. If IISMinimal is False for some constraints, the IIS is approximate and removing those constraints may not resolve infeasibility. Either increase the time limit or manually verify.
Time-Limited IIS Completeness Check.condition: Triggered when computeIIS() is called with a time limit (or when the solver hits its default IIS time limit) on a large infeasible model, and the result is used to guide constraint relaxation or repair.

NonConvex=2 for Global Quadratics.definition: By default, Gurobi treats quadratics as convex; setting NonConvex=2 activates spatial branch‑and‑bound and convex relaxation cuts. Tight variable bounds are crucial for efficiency.
NonConvex=2 for Global Quadratics.condition: When the model includes any nonconvex quadratic expression (products of continuous variables, negative‑definite quadratic forms) and you require a proven global optimum.

Solver-Native Multi-Objective Control.definition: Using setObjectiveN, you can specify up to 15 objectives with distinct priorities and optional weights within the same priority. The solver then optimizes sequentially (lexicographic) or blends weights. This avoids manual loops of fixing primary objective with epsilon constraints, reducing solve time and ensuring correct handling of integer variables.
Solver-Native Multi-Objective Control.condition: Multiple objectives have a strict priority ordering (e.g., primary: minimize noise; secondary: minimize energy cost) and the optimization solver supports native multi‑objective (Gurobi 9+).

Efficient Constraint Formulation (MVar &.definition: Use addMVar to create vector variables and addMConstr with the @ operator to write A @ x <= b, especially for dense patterns such as flow conservation or time‑linked capacities. For sparse rows (degree‑1 assignments, simple bound couplings), use addLConstr passing explicit variable indices and coefficients to bypass expression‑tree overhead. Both approaches dramatically reduce model‑building time and code volume.
Efficient Constraint Formulation (MVar &.condition: When building many constraints that can be expressed compactly by matrix‑vector operations, or when adding a large number of very sparse linear constraints where each row contains only a few nonzeros.

Degeneracy Cycling Prevention via Simple.definition: Degeneracy can cause simplex to cycle without progress. Use Bland's rule (enter/leave by smallest index) or lexicographic pivoting to guarantee termination. In Gurobi, choose Method=1 (dual simplex) or Method=0 with SimplexPricing=2 (steepest edge) to reduce stalling. In column generation with a degenerate master, check that the pivot step θ > 0 before asserting improvement; otherwise a negative reduced cost may n...
Degeneracy Cycling Prevention via Simple.condition: When LPs contain many active constraints with zero reduced costs (e.g., tight time windows, resource‑balance equalities) leading to degenerate pivots and potential cycling, or when using reduced costs to check optimality in a degenerate LP.

Warm-Start Basis Reuse for Model Modific.definition: For a new variable, compute its reduced cost using the dual solution (c_j - π^T A_j). If negative, append the column and invoke primal simplex from the current basis. For a new violated inequality, add the slack variable to form a dual‑feasible basis (primal infeasible) and apply dual simplex. For a new equality, introduce an artificial variable with large penalty and run primal simplex. Perturbations to nonbasic...
Warm-Start Basis Reuse for Model Modific.condition: When adding a variable, inequality, or equality to an LP that already has an optimal basis, or when a single column coefficient changes slightly, to avoid resolving from scratch.

Callback-Driven Lazy Constraint Addition.definition: Start with the base model containing only essential constraints (e.g., degree constraints for TSP). In a MIPSOL callback, check each integer incumbent for violations. If a violated constraint is found, add it lazily via cbLazy. The solver re-optimizes and repeats. This keeps the model size manageable while guaranteeing feasibility.
Callback-Driven Lazy Constraint Addition.condition: When solving MIP models where a family of constraints (e.g., subtour elimination, cutting stock) is exponentially large but can be separated efficiently from integer incumbent solutions, and a compact base model exists.

MIP-Start Injection from Heuristic.definition: A greedy heuristic that iteratively picks the facility covering the most uncovered demands provides a feasible solution in polynomial time. This solution can be set as a MIP start (Start attribute) to warm-start the solver, often reducing root-node processing. For uniform costs the greedy solution achieves an O(log n) approximation bound, guaranteeing a reasonable initial objective value.
MIP-Start Injection from Heuristic.condition: When the problem can be formulated as a set covering model (e.g., binary variables select facilities to satisfy demand) and a feasible initial solution is needed to accelerate branch-and-bound.

Solution Pool Utilization.definition: Set the solver’s PoolSolutions parameter to capture multiple feasible solutions (e.g., 10). Use PoolGap to limit the suboptimality margin and PoolSearchMode to encourage diversity. After optimization, retrieve all solutions and evaluate them using additional metrics like resilience or social acceptability.
Solution Pool Utilization.condition: When the problem exhibits symmetry or flat objective landscapes, and planners need to compare alternative optimal or near‑optimal solutions to choose one that performs best on unmodeled criteria.

Fix-and-Dive Primal Heuristic.definition: After the root LP, sort integer variables by fractionality (distance to the nearest integer). Fix the first quartile to that integer by setting both lower and upper bounds. The solver reuses the previous basis as warm start because variable indices remain. Re‑optimize (LP or MIP). Iterate until integer‑feasible or infeasible. The bound adjustments are temporary and can be reverted later. This avoids model rebuilding and exploits the solver’s warm‑start capability.
Fix-and-Dive Primal Heuristic.condition: When a large MIP yields a fractional LP relaxation with many near‑integer values and a primal bound is needed rapidly; do not use if the LP solution is highly fractional or the MIP is small enough to solve exactly.

Efficient Constraint Addition using Gene.definition: In GurobiPy, model.addConstrs((sum(flow[w,p] for w in W) <= cap[p]*open[p] for p in P), name='cap') adds all constraints in one call, which is faster than a for‑loop with addConstr. Use generator to avoid storing temporary lists.
Efficient Constraint Addition using Gene.condition: When constructing a model that requires a large family of identical structure constraints (e.g., capacity, demand) over index sets.

Presolve-Induced Dual Invisibility.definition: Gurobi's presolve can discard redundant integer variables, reducing MIP dimension but possibly breaking the logic of external components that expect those variables. To retain original integrality, set Presolve=0. Alternatively, record the presolved dimensions and adjust downstream logic accordingly.
Presolve-Induced Dual Invisibility.condition: When the model depends on a specific set of integer variables for custom branching, cut generation, or feasibility checks, and presolve might remove or relax them. Exclude for pure linear models without integrality sensitivity.

Presolve Disable for Raw Solver Behavior.definition: Presolve can scale rows/columns, remove roundoff‑prone constraints, or re‑express them in ways that hide underlying ill‑conditioning. Disabling presolve ensures that the solver works on the raw coefficient matrix, so any numerical warnings (high Kappa, large dual violations) directly reflect the formulation’s inherent quality. This is essential when designing robust formulations for thin feasible sets like UAM corridor separation constraints.
Presolve Disable for Raw Solver Behavior.condition: Use when you need to understand how the solver handles the exact, unscaled model, e.g., during KappaExact checks or perturbation sensitivity tests. In normal production, presolve is beneficial and should remain on unless dual values are needed from the original constraints.

Callback-Based Primal Heuristic Injectio.definition: Set model.Params.Heuristics = 0 to disable built-in heuristics. In a callback (e.g., MIPNODE), obtain the relative LP solution (cbGetNodeRel) for binary variables. Apply a rounding threshold (e.g., >0.5 → 1, else 0) and check feasibility. Use cbSetSolution to inject the rounded solution. This can provide a valid upper bound earlier or accelerate branch-and-cut when custom domain knowledge exists.
Callback-Based Primal Heuristic Injectio.condition: Applies when standard MIP heuristics are turned off (e.g., Heuristics=0) and a problem-specific rounding rule can quickly construct a feasible solution from the current LP relaxation point. Not needed if default heuristics already find good solutions or if rounding is unlikely to yield feasibility.

Multi-Scenario Feature.definition: After setting NumScenarios and defining scenario-specific data (e.g., ScenNRhs), call optimize. Then, to get per-scenario results, iterate over scenario indices, set ScenarioNumber, and query ScenNObjVal and ScenNObjBound. Comparing ScenNObjVal against GRB.INFINITY identifies infeasible scenarios. This avoids separate solves per scenario and provides detailed scenario-wise output for reporting or analysis.
Multi-Scenario Feature.condition: When using Gurobi's multi-scenario feature to solve stochastic programs with discrete scenarios, and you need to retrieve the optimal objective value or bound for each scenario after a single solve.

Solver Tuning Sensitivity.definition: Tuned solver settings are sensitive to the problem's matrix and variable distribution. A change like a new wake-separation minimum can alter the effect of cuts and heuristics, potentially increasing solve time. Use the solver's automatic tuning tool on a representative set of instances after structural modifications.
Solver Tuning Sensitivity.condition: When the problem structure changes—e.g., adding separation constraints, changing fleet composition, or modifying objective weights—do not assume previously tuned solver parameters remain effective; re-tune or revert to baseline.

Constraint-Guided Primal Heuristic.definition: Temporarily set lower and upper bounds of selected binary variables to the hinted value. Run Gurobi's NoRel heuristic (or equivalent) to extend the partial assignment into a full feasible solution. Restore the original variable bounds and inject the found solution as a MIP start. This acts as a lightweight feasibility pump without permanent model changes.
Constraint-Guided Primal Heuristic.condition: When a large MIP is infeasible to start and a credible partial assignment from domain knowledge exists.

Multi-Start for Nonconvex NLP.definition: Generate multiple feasible initial points (e.g., by perturbing a heuristic solution or sampling). Solve the NLP from each point using MIP starts or sequential solves. Retain the solution with the best objective. This multi‑start strategy mitigates the local‑only guarantee of the barrier method.
Multi-Start for Nonconvex NLP.condition: When solving a nonconvex NLP with barrier, where a single solve may yield a poor local optimum.

Callback Interface Compatibility.definition: Gurobi callbacks are not supported in MATLAB or R, and Compute Server/Instant Cloud have restrictions (e.g., no user callbacks). When building a model that relies on callbacks for lazy constraint generation or heuristic injection, use a Python, C++, Java, or .NET API and run on a local Gurobi license to ensure full callback functionality.
Callback Interface Compatibility.condition: Trigger: model uses callbacks for lazy constraints, heuristic, or logging. Avoid MATLAB/R API and cloud/distributed deployments if callbacks are essential; prefer C, C++, Java, .NET, Python local license.

Fixed MIP Dual Extraction.definition: Solve MIP, then fix all integer/binary variables to their optimal values, call m.fixed() to obtain a continuous LP, optimize it, and query Pi attributes. The duals reflect the marginal value of relaxing constraints given the fixed integer configuration, not the true MIP shadow price. Use with caution.
Fixed MIP Dual Extraction.condition: Applies when MIP duals are required for marginal cost analysis, Benders cut generation, or capacity valuation, but the solver natively offers only LP duals.

Multi-Scenario Baseline Robustness Test.definition: Fix discrete variables to the baseline values, set NumScenarios, and define scenario-specific RHS via ScenNRhs. After solving, the solver returns scenario-wise objective values and can report which scenarios are infeasible, providing a robustness profile without manual loops.
Multi-Scenario Baseline Robustness Test.condition: Applies when you have a baseline solution and need to assess its feasibility and cost variability across discrete scenarios; uses solver's native multi-scenario support to avoid model duplication.

Exact Condition Number Monitoring.definition: KappaExact computes the exact condition number of the optimal basis matrix. Large values signal that small perturbations in RHS or objective coefficients can produce large changes in the solution. This warns the modeler that the formulation needs scaling or that reported dual values are not trustworthy. Checking KappaExact is a fast diagnostic to decide whether to apply column/row scaling or to tighten Big‑M values before trusting the solution.
Exact Condition Number Monitoring.condition: Use whenever numerical reliability is critical and coefficients vary widely, or after observing unexpected dual/feasibility violations. High KappaExact (>1e9) strongly indicates that the optimal basis is ill-conditioned and the solution may be inaccurate.

Reduced-Price Fixing Heuristic.definition: If a variable’s absolute reduced cost (in the minimisation LP) is larger than the gap between the incumbent and the best bound, changing its value would at least increase the LP objective by that amount, making any new solution worse than the incumbent. Fixing it eliminates branching on that variable.
Reduced-Price Fixing Heuristic.condition: When a MIP has an incumbent solution and a non‑zero optimality gap; reduced costs from the LP relaxation can be used to permanently fix variables, shrinking the branch‑and‑bound tree.

MIP Solver Performance.definition: Explicitly define a binary variable for the condition and link it with indicator constraints (e.g., capacity_used = C ⇒ saturate = 1). Although this increases model size, it provides strong candidates for branching, often dramatically reducing search time because the solver can branch on these meaningful dichotomies instead of relying on generic variable branching.
MIP Solver Performance.condition: A MIP contains natural logical conditions (e.g., 'is a resource saturated?', 'is a flight delayed?') that are not encoded as variables, and the solver struggles to prove optimality due to poor branching decisions.

Sensitivity Sweep for Critical Fixed Par.definition: A single parameter like t_w can drastically reduce profit; without stress testing the optimal network configuration may be fragile. Sweeping across 0–20 minutes reveals the threshold where coverage becomes unprofitable, guides operational improvement targets, and highlights sensitivity for decision‑makers.
Sensitivity Sweep for Critical Fixed Par.condition: The model contains a fixed parameter (e.g., pre‑flight waiting time) that strongly influences the objective and whose true value is uncertain; the model is re‑solvable in reasonable time for multiple values.

Scenario-Contingent Variable Upper Bound.definition: Instead of adding scenario‑specific constraints, set the upper bound of the binary open variable to 0 via model.setAttr('ScenNUB', [open[p]], [0], s). This enforces closure directly, preserving model sparsity and avoiding duplicate constraints.
Scenario-Contingent Variable Upper Bound.condition: When modeling discrete scenarios where a facility (plant) must be closed in certain scenarios, and the model already uses Gurobi’s multi‑scenario feature.

Network Flow Reformulation for Efficienc.definition: Many large LPs are actually transshipment problems. By casting them as minimum-cost network flow (nodes with supply/demand, arcs with costs/capacities), you can use network simplex or specialized codes that exploit the totally unimodular node-arc incidence matrix for faster pivots. Even in general-purpose solvers, the network structure may be auto-detected and solved faster; explicitly identifying it aids algorithm selection.
Network Flow Reformulation for Efficienc.condition: When a distribution, transportation, or supply chain LP involves only flow conservation at nodes and arc capacities, reformulate it as a pure network flow problem to leverage network-optimized solvers or algorithms, greatly reducing solution time on large instances.

Data-Model Separation for Reusability.definition: Load data from CSV/JSON into dictionaries before model building. Use those dicts in all constraint expressions and objective terms. This avoids embedding numbers in code and makes the model instantly reusable for new instances.
Data-Model Separation for Reusability.condition: When the model must be re‑run with different demand, cost, or capacity inputs, e.g., sensitivity analysis or scenario studies.

Flat Scalar Index and ASCII Naming Requi.definition: Gurobi's addVars requires flat scalar indices. Nested tuples cause errors. Instead, flatten composite keys to strings (e.g., 'i_j') or use integer encoding. Constraint names must be ASCII without spaces; otherwise LP file export fails silently or with cryptic errors. Apply these rules at construction time to avoid debugging multi-index models.
Flat Scalar Index and ASCII Naming Requi.condition: When variable indices are naturally composite (e.g., (i,j) tuples) and you are tempted to pass tuples directly to addVars; or when constraint names contain spaces or non-ASCII characters for readability.
